name: Neugebauer-Meinel Disc of Dust
description: A disc of dust turning rigidly about its axis and held up by rotation alone, the exact solution of Einstein's equations, inside and out, that Gernot Neugebauer and Reinhard Meinel found between 1993 and 1995. Its one parameter runs from the Maclaurin disc of Newton's theory to a limit where the field outside the disc is the extreme Kerr black hole's.
convention: We keep factors of $c$ explicit, and the Ricci tensor is the standard contraction, $R_{\mu\nu} = R^\alpha{}_{\mu\alpha\nu}$. The disc has the coordinate radius $\rho_0$ and turns at the angular velocity $\Omega$, light from its centre reaches infinity with the redshift $e^{-V_0} - 1$, and $\mu = 2\Omega^2\rho_0^2e^{-2V_0}/c^2$.
history: Picture a record on a turntable, made of dust: grains that pull on one another by gravity alone, each on a circle about the axis, all turning at one angular velocity [neugebauer1993, neugebauer1996]. Rotation is all that keeps the grains from falling to the centre [bardeen1969]. In Newton's theory this is the Maclaurin disc, the Maclaurin spheroid flattened all the way [neugebauer1996]. To James Bardeen and Robert Wagoner, writing in 1969, it was "the simplest possible sort of rapidly rotating object", and the only known solution of Einstein's equations that could be the field of a rotating object was then Roy Kerr's vacuum metric [bardeen1969]. What becomes of the disc when it turns so fast that its gravity grows strong?¶Bardeen and Wagoner went after the answer by successive approximation, starting from Newton's disc [bardeen1969]. They wrote the metric as a power series in $\gamma = Z_c/(1 + Z_c)$, with $Z_c$ the redshift of light from the centre of the disc, and each of the two did the calculation independently, by a different numerical technique [bardeen1969]. Most of their results stayed accurate up to $\gamma = 1$, where the redshift is infinite [bardeen1971]. There the coordinate radius of the disc went to zero while its proper radius stayed finite, and its binding energy came to 37.3 percent of its rest mass [bardeen1969, bardeen1971]. Far from the disc the field became that of Kerr's black hole with $cJ = GM^2$, the largest angular momentum $J$ for a Kerr hole of mass $M$ [bardeen1971, meinel2002]. "There may be some hope of finding an analytic solution," they wrote [bardeen1969].¶Gernot Neugebauer and Reinhard Meinel found that solution in Jena, between 1993 and 1995 [neugebauer1993, neugebauer1995]. Their tool was the inverse scattering method of soliton physics, carried over from 1978 to 1980 to Einstein's vacuum equations for stationary fields with an axis of symmetry, Neugebauer among those who did it [neugebauer1993, neugebauer1979]. How does a method for empty space find the field of a body? A disc this thin has no interior, "it just consists of surface, so to say", and the dust enters as a boundary condition on the vacuum around it [neugebauer1996]. In the frame that turns with the disc the condition is that Frederick Ernst's potential take one constant value, $e^{2V_0}$, all over the disc [neugebauer1993, ernst1968]. By 1993 the two had turned the problem into a pair of linear integral equations, a "small" one for the axis of symmetry and a "big" one for everywhere else [neugebauer1993].¶By 1994 they had solved the small equation, in elliptic functions, and with it they had the potential on the axis and the metric and the density of the disc itself [neugebauer1994, neugebauer1995]. The big one took them one more year [neugebauer1995]. The answer needed functions older than relativity: it rests on an inversion problem that Carl Gustav Jacob Jacobi formulated in 1832, and it is written in ultraelliptic functions, theta functions of two variables [neugebauer1995, meinel1996]. Neugebauer and Meinel judged that it "seems to be the first rigorous global solution of the rotating body problem" in general relativity [neugebauer1995]. For rotating stars with an interior there was still no such solution in 2002, when Meinel wrote that their models "can only be treated by numerical methods so far" [meinel2002].¶One number fixes the whole family, $\mu = 2\Omega^2\rho_0^2e^{-2V_0}/c^2$, for a disc of coordinate radius $\rho_0$ turning at the angular velocity $\Omega$ [neugebauer1995, neugebauer1996]. A small $\mu$ gives back the Maclaurin disc [neugebauer1995]. Above $\mu = 1.68849$ the disc has an ergoregion, a torus in which every observer is dragged around the axis in the disc's direction of rotation [neugebauer1996, meinel2002]. The solution stays regular up to $\mu_0 = 4.62966184\ldots$, where the redshift from the centre becomes infinite [neugebauer1995, neugebauer1996]. A disc with a fixed number of baryons that loses energy would run through the family toward that end, shrinking and turning faster, what Meinel called a "parametric collapse" [neugebauer2003, meinel2002]. By the end it has given up 37.328 percent of its rest mass, and Bardeen and Wagoner's Padé approximants had said 37.323 [neugebauer1993].¶What remains at $\mu_0$? For an observer at any fixed distance the disc shrinks to a point, and the field around it is exactly the extreme Kerr metric, with the disc's angular velocity as the angular velocity of the horizon [meinel2002, neugebauer1996]. Neugebauer and Meinel had announced as much in 1993: "This proves a conjecture of Bardeen & Wagoner" [neugebauer1993]. The disc itself goes on existing, with a proper circumference of $4\pi\sqrt{\mu_0/2 - 1}\,GM/c^2$, in a space that is regular and is not flat far away [meinel2002]. An infinite proper distance separates the two regions, down the throat of the extreme Kerr hole, which Bardeen and Gary Horowitz studied on its own in 1999 [meinel2002, bardeen1999]. Meinel's theorem of 2004 makes the disc's end the rule: the extreme Kerr black hole is "the only candidate for a black hole limit of rotating fluid bodies in equilibrium" [meinel2004].

related.text: The field outside the disc in the limit $\mu \to \mu_0$. The disc shrinks to the origin of Weyl's coordinates, and everywhere else the metric is Kerr's at $J = GM^2/c$, with the disc's angular velocity as the horizon's [meinel2002].

The far side of the disc's own neighbourhood at $\mu_0$. Seen from the disc the space is regular and is not flat far away, where it becomes the throat of the extreme Kerr black hole [meinel2002, bardeen1971].

Another solution from Gernot Neugebauer's inverse methods in Jena: two Kerr black holes on one axis, made by Bäcklund transformations of flat space fifteen years before the disc was solved as a boundary value problem [kramer1980, neugebauer2003].

Discs of dust with as many grains turning one way as the other, so that nothing drags the frames. Bardeen and Wagoner set their disc beside it: the two agree in Newton's limit, and Morgan and Morgan's binding energy peaks near 5 percent of the rest mass where the rigidly rotating disc's climbs to 37 [bardeen1969, bardeen1971].

Dust that reaches a black hole by falling, a ball with no rotation whose outside is Schwarzschild's. The disc reaches the extreme Kerr black hole through a sequence of equilibria, which Meinel set beside this collapse as two idealized routes to a black hole [meinel2002].
A rotating star by approximation in slow rotation. Bardeen and Wagoner took up the disc because studies such as Hartle and Thorne's had assumed slow rotation or weak fields [bardeen1969].
Dust in rigid rotation again, as an infinite cylinder held up by its rotation alone [vanstockum1937]. The disc is the finite body of that kind, with flat space far away [neugebauer1995].

coordinates.name: Weyl-Lewis-Papapetrou

parameters.description: Dimensionless function of $\rho$ and $z$, with $-e^{2U}$ the norm of the Killing vector $\partial_t$ in the chart $x^0 = ct$; off the disc the spacetime is a vacuum, where the Ernst potential $f = e^{2U} + ib$ solves $e^{2U}\left(\partial_\rho^2f + \dfrac{1}{\rho}\partial_\rho f + \partial_z^2f\right) = \left(\partial_\rho f\right)^2 + \left(\partial_z f\right)^2$, and for the disc $f$ is Neugebauer and Meinel's quotient of ultraelliptic theta functions; inside the ergoregion, which the disc has for $\mu > 1.68849$, $e^{2U}$ is negative

Function of $\rho$ and $z$, a length, with $-a\,e^{2U}$ the product of the Killing vectors $\partial_t$ and $\partial_\phi$; off the disc $\partial_\rho a = \rho\,e^{-4U}\partial_z b$ and $\partial_z a = -\rho\,e^{-4U}\partial_\rho b$, where $b$ is the imaginary part of the Ernst potential, and $a = 0$ on the axis

Dimensionless function of $\rho$ and $z$, zero on the axis and fixed off the disc by $\partial_\rho k = \rho\left(\left(\partial_\rho U\right)^2 - \left(\partial_z U\right)^2 + \dfrac{e^{-4U}}{4}\left(\left(\partial_\rho b\right)^2 - \left(\partial_z b\right)^2\right)\right)$ and $\partial_z k = 2\rho\left(\partial_\rho U\,\partial_z U + \dfrac{e^{-4U}}{4}\partial_\rho b\,\partial_z b\right)$

coordinates.convention: We use the coordinates of Weyl, Lewis, and Papapetrou, $(t, \rho, z, \phi)$, as Neugebauer and Meinel write them, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time, and the disc is $z = 0$, $\rho \le \rho_0$. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, so $\dot{t}$ in the geodesic equations means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

parameters.description: Dimensionless function of $\rho$ and $z$, with $-e^{2U}$ the norm of $\partial_t$ at fixed $\varphi$, the Killing vector that follows the dust; on the disc $e^{2U} = e^{2V_0}$ at every radius, off it the Ernst potential $f = e^{2U} + ib$ of this frame solves $e^{2U}\left(\partial_\rho^2f + \dfrac{1}{\rho}\partial_\rho f + \partial_z^2f\right) = \left(\partial_\rho f\right)^2 + \left(\partial_z f\right)^2$, and $e^{2U}$ falls through zero on the surface where a point at rest in the frame moves at the speed of light

Function of $\rho$ and $z$, a length, with $-a\,e^{2U}$ the product of the Killing vectors $\partial_t$ and $\partial_\varphi$; off the disc $\partial_\rho a = \rho\,e^{-4U}\partial_z b$ and $\partial_z a = -\rho\,e^{-4U}\partial_\rho b$, where $b$ is the imaginary part of the Ernst potential of this frame, which vanishes on the disc, and $\partial_z a = 0$ on the disc

Dimensionless function of $\rho$ and $z$, zero on the axis, with $k - U$ the same in this frame and in the frame at rest far away; off the disc $\partial_\rho k = \rho\left(\left(\partial_\rho U\right)^2 - \left(\partial_z U\right)^2 + \dfrac{e^{-4U}}{4}\left(\left(\partial_\rho b\right)^2 - \left(\partial_z b\right)^2\right)\right)$ and $\partial_z k = 2\rho\left(\partial_\rho U\,\partial_z U + \dfrac{e^{-4U}}{4}\partial_\rho b\,\partial_z b\right)$

coordinates.convention: We use the coordinates $(t, \rho, z, \varphi)$ of the frame that turns with the disc, $\varphi = \phi - \Omega t$ with $\phi$ the angle of an observer at rest far away, and $t$ carries dimensions of time. The functions $U$, $a$, and $k$ are the $U'$, $a'$, and $k'$ of Neugebauer and Meinel, and the disc is $z = 0$, $\rho \le \rho_0$. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, so $\dot{t}$ in the geodesic equations means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.
